{"id": "74:16/q14", "question": "Can an unbeliever receive God's favor in the sense at issue here?", "turns_on": "Whether favors granted in this life count as God's favor to an unbeliever in the disputed sense.", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q14/p1", "position": "Yes, an unbeliever may receive God's favor.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports this as the view of al-Maturidi and the Mu'tazilites."}, {"id": "74:16/q14/p2", "position": "No, an unbeliever does not receive God's favor in this sense.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports al-Ash'ari's differing view."}, {"id": "74:16/q14/p3", "position": "The disagreement over favor to unbelievers is verbal.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur follows careful scholars who frame the difference as one of wording."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q15", "question": "What does the opponents' response reveal about the Qur'an's inimitability?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q15/p1", "position": "Their resort to insults and fighting, despite intense opposition, shows they could not meet the Qur'an's challenge.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi uses the enemies' failure to rebut the challenge as evidence of inimitability."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q16", "question": "Can reflection or thought be bad?", "turns_on": "Whether intent to invalidate truth can make reflection bad.", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q16/p1", "position": "Yes: thought aimed at invalidating truth can be bad.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi says describing unbelief as an attempt to invalidate truth supports Abu Hashim and argues against Abu Ali."}, {"id": "74:16/q16/p2", "position": "Abu Ali's opposed view denies that reflection can be bad in this way.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi names Abu Ali as the opponent of Abu Hashim's account, but supplies no separate argument for him."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q17", "question": "Who performs the thinking and grimacing described in this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q17/p1", "position": "The human servant performs these acts.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi explicitly attributes the thinking and grimacing to the servant."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q18", "question": "How does al-Muddaththir relate to al-Muzzammil?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q18/p1", "position": "It is the preceding surah's counterpart, with essentially the same central themes and a similarly meaningful name.", "reasons": "Islahi draws the connection between their themes and names."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q19", "question": "What is the warning of verses 11–17?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q19/p1", "position": "Judgment will be severe for disbelievers who assume wealth and rank promise further gain.", "reasons": "Islahi says the affluent man's expected increase is false; opposing the Qur'an instead brings severe penalty. {"id": "74:16/q20", "question": "How do other verses portray Meccan opposition to the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q20/p1", "position": "They record repeated allegations that it was human fabrication, ancient lore, or copied writings, and argue against those claims.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati cites 68:10–15, 44–47; 25:4–10; 17:87–96; 6:7–9, 25–26; and 34:43–45 as parallels and rebuttals."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q21", "question": "How do the later verses explain the charge that he opposed God's signs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q21/p1", "position": "His thinking and devising explains and completes the statement that he was obstinate toward God's signs.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reads the account of his thinking and devising as an explanation and completion of 74:16."}]}
{"id": "74:16/q22", "question": "How do the threats in this passage correspond to his conduct?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:16/q22/p1", "position": "The worldly threat answers his pursuit of leadership and envy; Hell answers his attack on the Qur'an and denial of revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur connects his worldly motives with the worldly threat and his attacks on revelation with the threat of Hell, referring to 74:14 and 74:24–26."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q01", "question": "What does سأصليه mean in this threat?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is being explained in its punitive context or by its wider attested usage around fire.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q01/p1", "position": "God will put him into the Fire, exposing him to its flames and heat.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, al-Wajīz, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explain it as admission to Hell. Al-Jishumī says iṣlāʾ consigns someone to the fire's place and has a root sense of staying or sticking there; he and al-Ṭabrisī add that the person remains there, al-Jishumī saying perpetually. Al-Biqāʿī calls the threat inevitable and soon to arrive. Asad places the suffering in the life to come. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites burning uses at 111:3, 92:14–15, and 4:10."}, {"id": "74:26/q01/p2", "position": "The verb can also describe warming oneself by a fire.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza's poetry for ṣilāʾ as experiencing fire's heat for warmth, and Ḥamīd ibn Thawr's line lā taṣṭalī al-nāra for the same usage; he also gives burning as a sense used in this threat."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q02", "question": "Whose conduct prompts this threat?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate trigger is characterized as obstinate plotting generally or the specific slander of the Qurʾān.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q02/p1", "position": "The threatened person is the disbeliever just described, whose obstinacy and plotting incur punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the passage follows mention of the disbeliever with a threat. Al-Biqāʿī connects the heat attacking and melting the brain to the man's mental plotting to burn God's friends, and connects the preceding Ṣaʿūd punishment with his obstinacy. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the earlier fa in 'then he said' marks his immediate speech once intense deliberation produced the thought."}, {"id": "74:26/q02/p2", "position": "The threat answers his slander that the Qurʾān is transmitted magic or human speech.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān assigns this Saqar threat to his claim about transmitted magic, after an earlier threat for defiance of the signs. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports an explanation that the threat confirms the preceding denial that the Qurʾān is human speech. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ surveys related accusations of outside help, copied ancient tales, bewitchment, and missing angelic or worldly signs at 25:4–10, 17:87–96, 6:7–9 and 6:25–26, and 34:43–45; she says the Qurʾān answers with revelation, God's knowledge, and earlier messengers. Ibn ʿĀshūr links the threat of Hell specifically to the man's attacks on the Qurʾān and denial of revelation, following 74:24–25."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q03", "question": "What does سقر denote?", "turns_on": "Whether Saqar names Hell as a whole, a level or gate within it, a specified part, or an allegorical name for afterlife suffering; reports disagree over its numbered location.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q03/p1", "position": "Saqar is a name for Hell or its Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares the proper name Laẓā. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the majority of commentators use it synonymously with Jahannam, although it can name a place within Hell. Ibn al-Jawzī refers readers to 54:48. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows this alongside a level; the Turkish commentary cites al-Shawkānī for a name of the fire that also denotes a section with severe punishment."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p2", "position": "Saqar is an unspecified level or section of Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this alongside gate and name interpretations. Al-Ṭabrisī reports a level as an alternative to Hell and its gate. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows a named place in Hell; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows one of its levels. The Turkish commentary reports al-Shawkānī's description of a section with severe punishment; al-Biqāʿī describes a fiery level whose heat melts the brain."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p3", "position": "Saqar is the sixth level or depth of Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr transmit this from Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the sixth level; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that Ibn ʿAṭiyya confines his explanation to the sixth depth."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p4", "position": "Saqar is an unspecified gate of Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī lists a gate among reported explanations; al-Ṭabrisī reports it as an alternative, and the Study Quran cites al-Ṭabarī for it."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p5", "position": "Saqar is Hell's fifth gate.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies the fifth gate."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p6", "position": "Saqar is the lowest part of Hell, containing the tree of Zaqqūm.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Durr al-Manthūr; it differs in detail from the sixth-level reports also attributed to him."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p7", "position": "Saqar is one of seven metaphorical names for self-incurred suffering in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Asad calls this its earliest Qurʾānic occurrence and attributes that suffering to sin and deliberate blindness to spiritual truth, mentioning 15:33; he reads descriptions here and from 74:28 onward allegorically."}]}

{"id": "74:26/q05", "question": "Why is سقر not declined?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q05/p1", "position": "It is a feminine proper name, so it is diptote.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ calls it a proper name like Laẓā; al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite proper naming and feminine gender. {"id": "74:26/q06", "question": "Why choose the word سقر?", "turns_on": "The notes offer semantic force and the Qurʾān's choice of a rarer rhyming synonym as different explanations of the wording.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q06/p1", "position": "Its fierce scorching sense suits the threatened punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the name reflects the fire's intense pain; al-Biqāʿī ties its brain-melting heat to the man's plotting to burn God's friends."}, {"id": "74:26/q06/p2", "position": "The Qurʾān may favor this rarer synonym to preserve the sūra's rhyme.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī gives Saqar among rare synonymous choices with ḍīzā, al-ḥuṭama, Laẓā, and Hāwiya, and says rhyme often motivates such choices."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q07", "question": "How does this threat relate to the earlier threat of Ṣaʿūd?", "turns_on": "The syntactic link to 74:17 and surrounding statements, especially whether Ṣaʿūd is hardship or a physical mountain, and whether the two threats answer separate offenses.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q07/p1", "position": "It explains or substitutes for the earlier threat, with Saqar encompassing the ascent or its hardships.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī treats it as substitution for 74:17, as reported by Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn; al-Kashshāf itself says it replaces the earlier promise. Al-Nasafī says it explains that promise. Al-Samīn finds substitution clear if Ṣaʿūd means hardship, harder if it is a rock in Hell, except as a part-whole relation. Al-Bursawī calls Saqar an inclusionary apposition whether Ṣaʿūd is hardships or a mountain of fire. Al-Ālūsī calls it a partitive substitution because Saqar contains severe ordeals and, on one reading, a mountain of fire. Elmalılı calls it explication and an inclusive substitute. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports substitution as one possibility; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the clause explains or apposes 74:17."}, {"id": "74:26/q07/p2", "position": "The two are successive threats for two stages of the man's conduct.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān associates Ṣaʿūd with obstinacy toward the signs and Saqar with calling the Qurʾān transmitted magic; al-Ālūsī reports this division but objects that the preceding discussion makes it problematic. Al-Biqāʿī describes the earlier obstinacy and Ṣaʿūd punishment, followed by naming Saqar as the afterlife recompense. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes an earlier worldly threat responding to the man's worldly motives of leadership and envy from the Hell threat responding to his attacks on the Qurʾān and denial of revelation."}, {"id": "74:26/q07/p3", "position": "It begins a new explanatory sentence prompted by the account of thought and calculation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives this as an alternative to substitution, referring to the preceding account at 74:18."}, {"id": "74:26/q07/p4", "position": "It confirms the preceding denial that the Qurʾān is human speech, despite a difference in meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports that some take the clauses as uncoordinated because both convey that denial."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q08", "question": "How do the surrounding verses heighten or recall Saqar's threat?", "turns_on": "The notes address different surrounding clauses, one describing Saqar's dread and another possibly referring back to it.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q08/p1", "position": "The wording and following question magnify Saqar's dread.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says the wording magnifies its dread. Ibn ʿĀshūr parses 'What will make you know what Saqar is?' as a circumstantial clause modifying Saqar and says no informant could make its reality known to the Prophet, magnifying its dreadful state."}, {"id": "74:26/q08/p2", "position": "A later feminine pronoun may refer back to Saqar as a reminder through its threat and horrors.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this as another possibility, with an omitted noun such as Saqar's mention or description understood."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q09", "question": "What does a report say about the inhabitant of Saqar?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q09/p1", "position": "God told Moses that the inhabitant of Saqar is the poorest servant.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits Abū Hurayra's account of Moses asking God which servant is poorest and God's reply; al-Thaʿlabī supplies no grading."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q10", "question": "What does the verse's punishment teach in the sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes draw distinct lessons from the threat: inescapability, personal moral causation, and the response of truth-seekers versus mockers.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q10/p1", "position": "The disbelievers cannot escape the horrors of Hell's punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the sūra's terrors and says the passage makes disbelievers despair of escape."}, {"id": "74:26/q10/p2", "position": "Sin and deliberate blindness bring afterlife suffering on the person himself; its descriptions are allegorical.", "reasons": "Asad calls Saqar one of seven metaphorical names for this suffering, points to 15:33, and reads this passage and the descriptions from 74:28 onward allegorically."}, {"id": "74:26/q10/p3", "position": "The description rests on divine wisdom: truth-seekers benefit, while arrogant mockers ruin their fate.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says disbelievers mock the description of Hell because they assume they know everything; the differing effects on sincere and arrogant readers express divine wisdom."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q11", "question": "Which other infernal terms are discussed alongside Saqar?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish a list of rarer synonymous words from a list of specifically named valleys.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q11/p1", "position": "Some rare Qurʾānic terms are treated as synonyms in a discussion including Saqar.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī lists ḍīzā, al-ḥuṭama, Saqar, Laẓā, and Hāwiya as rarer synonymous choices, often serving the sūra's rhyme."}, {"id": "74:26/q11/p2", "position": "Several other named terms are classified as valleys in Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī lists Ghayy, Atham, Mwbq, Saʿīr, Wayl, Saʾil, and Suhaq as valleys. He reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's more specific description of Saʿīr as a valley of pus and Suhaq as a valley in Hell. These notes do not classify Saqar as a valley."}]}
{"id": "74:29/q01", "question": "What does لَوَّاحَةٌۭ describe Saqar as doing or showing?", "turns_on": "Whether the root describes scorching alteration, visible appearance, or thirst; whether the effect is physical or allegorical; and whether 'it leaves nothing' in 74:28 permits skin merely to blacken.", "positions": [{"id": "74:29/q01/p1", "position": "Saqar scorches, burns, alters, and darkens human skin or appearance.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd and many later commentators describe burning or changed complexions. Abū Razīn and others say its blast leaves skin darker than night; al-Māwardī's ʿAṭiyya says it burns until bone shows. Ibn Zayd cites exposure to sky; Ibn Qutayba, al-Layth, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī and others compare sun, heat, cold, illness, thirst or grief changing appearance. Abū ʿUbayda, al-Aʿshā and other poetic lines attest the verb; al-Kashshāf cites a scorching poem, and al-Itqān identifies Azd Shanūʾa usage. Al-Jishumī and Elmalılı stress the intensive form; al-Biqāʿī adds blueness, flashing, convulsion and thirst. Al-Wāḥidī says 'burning' names the effect while the fuller sense is piercing alteration to blackness. Al-Islāḥī says the flames reach criminals from afar and cites 70:16. Al-Qāshānī relates the outward blackening to sins and dispositions. Al-Ṭabarī suspects an Ibn ʿAbbās report reading 'exposed' is a copyist's error for 'changed'. Ibn ʿĀshūr derives lawwāḥa from lawḥ, alteration of a person's substance through pain; he cites an unidentified poet's line in which scorching winds change a traveler. He also says the Fire turns human skin black."}, {"id": "74:29/q01/p2", "position": "Saqar shines or becomes visible to people, even from five hundred years away.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Kaysān and others give the five-hundred-year distance; Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes visibility to its vast size, terror and roaring. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī compare a lightning-like gleam. Al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī cite 26:91; al-Kashshāf cites 102:7; al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī cite 79:36; Abū Ḥayyān cites 102:6 and 79:36. Kuranyolu also reports a tableau or mirror revealing Hell to one who deserves it. Study Quran says Saqar is made apparent

He compares the sinner's state of neither life nor death with 87:12–13."}]}
{"id": "74:29/q02", "question": "How is لَوَّاحَةٌۭ read and construed?", "turns_on": "The case ending and what earlier word or unspoken subject governs the description; the accusative also permits circumstance or emphatic specification.", "positions": [{"id": "74:29/q02/p1", "position": "It is read accusative, as a description of Saqar, a circumstantial expression, or emphatic specification.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others name ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī; Ibn al-Jawzī adds Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ and Ibn Abī ʿAbla; al-Qurṭubī names Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī name Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Abī ʿAbla. Al-Jishumī relates the adjective to Saqar under sa-uṣlīhi; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī relate the circumstance to Saqar or the pronoun under lā tubqī/lā tadhar. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bayḍāwī call it specification intensifying the threat; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn explain emphatic circumstance because a consuming fire necessarily alters skin. Al-Samīn says this reading supports treating lā tubqī as circumstantial."}, {"id": "74:29/q02/p2", "position": "The common nominative reads it as Saqar's adjective or as a predicate in a new clause with an omitted subject.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ supplies an implicit repeated Saqar and compares 85:15–16 and a reading of 11:72. Al-Ṭabarī permits an indefinite description as praise. Al-Naḥḥās, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī supply 'it is'; al-Samīn says the nominative supports an independent lā tubqī. Al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī relate the adjective to Saqar in 'what is Saqar?'; Abū Ḥayyān treats the majority reading as a fresh clause about scorching fire."}, {"id": "74:29/q02/p3", "position": "The nominative lawwāḥa is a third predicate of Saqar.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr construes it as Saqar's third predicate."}]}
{"id": "74:29/q03", "question": "What is the function of the lām in لِّلْبَشَرِ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:29/q03/p1", "position": "The lām is an added particle that strengthens the expression.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn compares the Yūsuf phrase in 12:43."}]}
{"id": "74:29/q04", "question": "Who or what is الْبَشَرِ?", "turns_on": "Whether bashar is the skin noun bashara in collective or plural use, or the human beings who are scorched or see Saqar.", "positions": [{"id": "74:29/q04/p1", "position": "It means human skin or its visible outer surface.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda and many commentators take it as skin or complexion. Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī call bashar a plural of bashara; al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Biqāʿī also report the plural abshār. Al-Jishumī says humans are called bashar because their skin is uncovered by fur; Elmalılı similarly connects the name with visible skin. Al-Kashshāf specifies upper skin layers, and Ibn al-Jawzī calls it the visible outer layer. {"id": "74:29/q05", "question": "How does this description relate to Saqar's leaving nothing in 74:28 and to nearby verses?", "turns_on": "Whether 'leaves nothing' excludes a lasting darkened skin, or allows stages, different subjects, or a further feature of punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "74:29/q05/p1", "position": "Blackening can precede destruction, affect those near the fire, or name one of its disfiguring effects.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī answers the apparent tension by making blackening precede burning and destruction, or distinguishing inmates from those nearby. {"id": "74:31/q01", "question": "Who are the companions of the Fire?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase denotes literal angelic guards, an elliptical construction, or allegorical human faculties.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q01/p1", "position": "The angels appointed to guard and administer Hell, rather than its inmates or human jailers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and others connect them to the nineteen over Saqar in 74:30; Bursevī contrasts the normal sense in 59:20; Elmalılı names Mālik as chief. {"id": "74:31/q03", "question": "What does their number count?", "turns_on": "Whether nineteen names individual chiefs, thousands, ranks, or an unspecified kind of count.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q03/p1", "position": "Nineteen individual angels, commonly understood as chiefs with many other angelic attendants.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites the majority and a report of seventy thousand reins each carried by seventy thousand angels; al-Nasafī notes Mālik as chief. {"id": "74:31/q04", "question": "Why exactly nineteen keepers?", "turns_on": "Whether the number's wisdom is inaccessible or can be derived from arithmetic, Hell's organization, or human faculties.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q04/p1", "position": "Its precise wisdom belongs to God's free choice and remains unknown to creatures.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares every finite body's determinate number and every event's determinate time; al-Ālūsī prefers consigning this ambiguous matter to God and criticizes speculative rationales. {"id": "74:31/q05", "question": "What makes the number a fitna for unbelievers?", "turns_on": "Whether fitna is epistemic testing through a surprising count, punitive consequence, empowered few, or a misread allegory.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q05/p1", "position": "The unexpectedly small number exposes unbelievers' mockery, denial, and assumption they can overpower the keepers.", "reasons": "Sources mention sneering at nineteen rather than twenty, its seeming inability to punish all jinn and humans, denial of resurrection, and reluctance to accept divine power. {"id": "74:31/q06", "question": "How is 'we made their number only a trial' constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether fitna names a cause through metonymy or the condition imposed on unbelievers.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q06/p1", "position": "Fitna is jaʿalnā's second object and denotes the cause or occasion of a trial, with effect named for cause.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn supply an omitted 'cause'; Bursevī says the number cannot literally equal the unbelievers' temptation; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī take the number's announcement as the effective making. {"id": "74:31/q07", "question": "What incident prompted the answer that the guards are angels?", "turns_on": "Which reported taunt and speaker elicited the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q07/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl mocked the nineteen and challenged Quraysh to overpower the guards; a strongman offered to take seventeen while others took two.", "reasons": "Accounts vary the strongman's name among Abū al-Ashadd, Abū al-Ashaddayn, Abū al-Asad and al-Ḥārith ibn Kalda; some report a ten-to-one challenge, a cowhide feat, or a boast of pushing ten right and nine left. {"id": "74:31/q08", "question": "What happened when Jews asked about Hell's keepers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q08/p1", "position": "They asked the Prophet or Companions the count; the Prophet indicated nineteen with his fingers and they affirmed it.", "reasons": "Jābir's versions vary between ten then nine and ten, ten, then nine; al-Barāʾ's version says revelation followed a Companion's deferral. {"id": "74:31/q09", "question": "Why do scripture recipients become certain?", "turns_on": "Whether certainty arises from a matching scriptural number, divine power, or an allegorical continuity.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q09/p1", "position": "The Qur'anic nineteen matches their Torah or Gospel, confirming the report, Muhammad's prophethood, and revelation's divine origin.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and many commentators transmit the scriptural count. {"id": "74:31/q15", "question": "Who are the unbelievers named beside the diseased-hearted?", "turns_on": "Whether these unbelievers are Meccan polytheists or denying scripture communities.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q15/p1", "position": "Meccan Arab polytheists or those openly fixed in denial.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī prefers Muqātil's Arab identification since scripture readers would not deny their own book; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Biqāʿī stress settled denial."}, {"id": "74:31/q15/p2", "position": "Jews and Christians.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports ʿAṭāʾ and al-Kalbī then rejects this against his Arab-polytheist reading; al-Qurṭubī reports it as the majority's view."}]}
{"id": "74:31/q16", "question": "What does the lām of 'so that they say' express?", "turns_on": "Whether their speech is a divine aim, an incidental consequence, or a prediction.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q16/p1", "position": "An eventual or unintended outcome, not the intended purpose of their objectionable speech.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazila, Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and others compare 28:8; al-Ālūsī distinguishes intended guidance from incidental misguidance and allows both clauses as consequence; Bursevī resolves the problem of God intending mockery this way."}, {"id": "74:31/q16/p2", "position": "A real divine purpose, since God can intend their response.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says his theological position allows this; al-Ṭabrisī reports a purpose by which questioning and reflection might lead to faith. {"id": "74:31/q22", "question": "How does God guide and misguide through this example?", "turns_on": "Whether God creates the response, reveals a chosen response through a test, withholds aid, judges it, or manifests primordial disposition.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q22/p1", "position": "God guides receptive believers and leaves mocking deniers astray according to His will and knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says God abandons some from truth and enables others; al-Rāzī says the verse supports his companions' doctrine and counters Muʿtazilī alternatives. {"id": "74:31/q25", "question": "What reports illustrate the multitude of God's angels?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q25/p1", "position": "Heaven is densely filled with worshipping angels, with many beyond human or even Gabriel's knowledge.", "reasons": "Reports vary: the sky groans with no finger, palm, handspan or foot space empty; seventy thousand enter Bayt al-Maʿmūr daily without return; Ismāʿīl commands twelve thousand with twelve thousand each or seventy thousand with one hundred thousand each; Moses hears of twelve tribes innumerable as dust.
